Thank you, Mr. Chair. We thank the Chair Rapporteur and the Secretary for convening this session. Japan also places great importance on advancing the right to education for all children. Japan has also been actively engaged in international cooperation in the field of education, providing wide range of support to strengthen education in developing countries. This includes supporting efforts to ensure the right to education of girls who are left behind in accessing education and learning opportunities, children with disabilities, and children in conflict-affected areas, as well as making contribution to international organizations. As we stated in our comments on the key principles submitted in May this year, Japan considers that it important, in line with the mandate set out in Human Rights Council resolution 56/5, to continue to fully explore the possibility of elaborating an optional protocol. While we see value in discussing the key principles, such discussions should not prejudge either the elaboration of an optional protocol or transition to the drafting phase. As we have stated previously, in considering a new optional protocol, it is necessary to carefully examine its relationship with existing international human rights treaties. In particular, with regard to secondary education, Article 13 of the ICESCR already provides for the progressive introduction of free education, while Article 28 of the CRC calls on States to take appropriate measures such as the introduction of free education and offering financial assistance in case of need. Against this background, it is important to carefully assess how a new instrument could complement existing obligations without duplicating them and what added value it could provide. In realizing the right to education, it is important to take fully into account the differences among States in their institutional frameworks, socioeconomic circumstances and available resources. With regard to the obligations set out in the KISS principles, it is also important to ensure consistency with the principles under the ICCPR of progressive realization and the maximum use of available resources. International cooperation plays an important role in advancing the realization of the right to education, and Japan continues to attach importance to international cooperation in the field of education. At the same time, we need to carefully consider how international cooperation should be addressed in an optional protocol, taking into account the responsibilities of states and the possible optional protocol's relationship with the existing framework of international law. Furthermore, if consideration of a draft optional protocol is to proceed, care should be taken to avoid making the obligations overly rigid, which could limit the number of States able to participate and as a result could undermine the universality and effectiveness of the instrument. It is also important to consider whether the framework would enable States to broadly participate and whether it would contribute in practice to realization of the right to education. In light of the above, Japan intends to engage constructively in discussions on the key principles while carefully listening to the views expressed by Member States at this session. We will continue to consider the most effective way forward, including the necessity of an optional protocol and the value it could provide. I thank you.
